lede_ma.html: Measured from 2020, New England's residential prices after inflation rose 22% more than the rest of the US outside PJM by 2023, and were still 10% ahead in 2026. Data centers are not the reason: Massachusetts has 67 MW of them operating and 300 MW proposed, and the capacity charge in a typical Massachusetts home's bill fell from $245 a year in 2018/19 to $84 for 2027/28.

lede_contrast.html: PJM, the grid operator for 13 states and DC from New Jersey to Illinois, shows what it looks like when data centers do drive the market: a capacity shortfall driven largely by forecast data center demand now costs a typical household in a restructured state about $196 a year more than in 2024/25. For 2027/28, the same charge is $242 there against $84 in Massachusetts.

ma_cap_reading.html: The capacity charge pays power plants to be available at peak, and in Massachusetts basic service passes ISO New England's auction price straight through. For a typical home it fell from $245 a year in 2018/19 to $52 in 2023/24, then $102, $64, and $84 for 2027/28. New England's auctions have little data center demand behind them: 0.7 GW planned or under construction across the region, against 132 GW in PJM.

ne_reading.html: New England prices tracked the rest of the country outside PJM in 2021, then rose 8.2% more in 2022 and 22.0% more in 2023, measured from 2020, and were still 10.0% above in 2026. Capacity charges fell over the same years ($118 to $52 per Massachusetts home), so the rise did not come through the capacity auction, the channel that carries data center costs in PJM.

Massachusetts' municipal utilities charged 16.5¢, about half, and the New England average was 27.6¢ against 16.7¢ nationally.

ma_supply_reading.html: 76% of homes at the three investor-owned utilities buy supply from a competitive supplier or their town's aggregation program (55% through towns, 21% individually), as of June 2026. On EIA's statewide averages, competitive suppliers charged more than basic service in 5 of 10 years from 2015 to 2024, and less in 3, by the most when basic service spiked (17.4¢ against 15.2¢ in 2023). Over the period, that is about $105 million less than basic service would have cost. That average mixes town aggregation, which buys in bulk, with individual contracts. The Attorney General's office, which studies individual contracts only, finds those households paid $738.7 million more than basic service from July 2015 to June 2025, $87.4 million of it in the latest year. Taken together, town aggregation, not individual contracts, is what kept the statewide average near or below basic service.

ma_dc_reading.html: Massachusetts has 25 data center sites in the merged list, 67 MW operating. Nearly all of the 300 MW in the pipeline is one proposal: Servistar Data Center in Hampden County (300 MW). New England as a whole has 137 MW operating and 669 MW proposed or under construction; PJM has 132 GW in its pipeline. ISO New England's own first large-load forecast (2026) counts one data center in its formal study process, 200 MW in the Northeast Massachusetts and Boston zone, and expects all large new loads together to add about 110 MW to the region's peak in the 2030s.

c1_reading.html: Capacity costs for a typical home fell to $32 a year in 2023/24, then jumped to $217 when the 2025/26 auction cleared at $269.92 per MW-day, and reached $242 as the 2026/27 to 2028/29 auctions cleared at the price cap. That is the highest level in the record, about 1.5 times 2018/19. The market monitor attributes roughly $96 to $137 a year of it to data center load.

That is the highest level in the record, about 1.5 times 2018/19. The market monitor attributes roughly $96 to $137 a year of it to data center load.

c1_compare.html: New England is the comparison. Its capacity auctions have little data center demand behind them (0.7 GW of data centers planned or under construction, against 132 GW in PJM), and a typical home's capacity cost there fell from $289 a year in 2018/19 to $93 in 2027/28, against $242 in restructured PJM.

c1_miso.html: In MISO, the central US grid, most utilities supply their own capacity, so auction prices reach household bills directly mainly at Ameren Illinois. There the cost has swung rather than climbed: $223 a year in 2022/23, $8 the next year, $204 in 2025/26 when the summer price hit $666.50 per MW-day, and $123 for 2026/27. MISO has 47 GW of data centers planned or under construction (2.9 MW per 1,000 homes, against 5.3 in PJM).

c1_ny.html: New York has little data center load (2.5 GW planned or under construction, 0.4 MW per 1,000 homes), yet New York City's capacity price, which sets most of Con Edison's cost, reached a record $32.59 per kW-month in May 2026 and averaged $19.14 over summer 2026. Statewide, a typical New York home's capacity cost was $125 a year for 2025/26.

rel_utility.html: What about reliability? Across 1,339 utilities (2013-2025), a 40% rise in a utility's own commercial load has not gone with more outages: −2.3% in everyday outage minutes per customer (95% CI −4.8% to +0.3%) and −1.8% in the number of outages, compared with utilities in the same regional grid and year. Including major storms, −4.6%.

m_capacity_ne.html: New England. ISO New England's Forward Capacity Auctions run three years ahead with the same June-to-May years. The region-wide price fell from $9.55 per kW-month for 2018/19 to $2.59 for 2026/27, then rose to $3.58 for 2027/28; the next auction, for 2028/29, is due in 2028 after a delay for market redesign. With the same method and New England's annual energy, a typical home's capacity cost fell from $289 a year to $93. All New England states but Vermont pass auction prices through default supply. No data center attribution has been published; the region has 0.7 GW of data centers planned or under construction, about 0.1 MW per 1,000 homes against 5.3 in PJM.

m_capacity_miso.html: MISO. MISO's Planning Resource Auction is held each spring for the coming June-to-May year, with separate summer, fall, winter, and spring prices since 2023/24; seasonal prices are weighted by days. Most MISO utilities are regulated and supply their own capacity, so the site applies auction prices only where default supply buys capacity in the auction: Ameren Illinois (Zone 4). Its typical home's cost ranged from $3 to $223 a year (2022/23); for 2026/27 it is $123. No data center attribution has been published.

m_capacity_ny.html: New York. NYISO buys capacity in seasonal and monthly auctions and a monthly spot auction, priced separately for New York City, Long Island, the lower Hudson Valley (the G-J Locality), and the rest of the state. The site averages the 12 monthly spot prices in each May-to-April capability year (complete years only, through 2025/26), read from NYISO's public auction viewer each week, and uses an approximate statewide requirement of 36 GW (forecast peak of about 31.5 GW plus the 18-24% installed reserve margin, less derating). All seven large New York utilities pass these costs through, including the Long Island Power Authority through its power supply charge. A typical home's cost ranged from $47 to $126 a year; Con Edison's peaked at $261 (2023/24). New York City's spot price reached $32.59 per kW-month in May 2026.

m_pjm.html: PJM vs. the rest of the US (2020 = 0): no difference from 2017 to 2021; +3.3% in 2022, +11.1% in 2023, +11.1% in 2024, +12.6% in 2025, +15.5% in 2026. The gap opened before capacity prices spiked, consistent with 2022 natural gas prices being locked into default-supply contracts, and widened as capacity costs reached bills from mid-2025.

m_pjm_restructured.html: Within PJM, restructured vs. regulated: +18.3% in 2026, but the two groups were not on parallel paths before 2020, so this comparison is weaker evidence.

m_rel_utility.html: A 40% rise in commercial load goes with −2.3% outage minutes (95% CI −4.8% to +0.3%) and −1.8% outages; including major storms, −4.6% (−7.5% to −1.6%). IEEE-only check: −0.7% (−4.1% to +2.9%). No sign that reliability has worsened where commercial load grew.

m_rel_county.html: The 31 counties with at least 10 MW of operating data center capacity per 1,000 households had the same or fewer outage hours than other counties in their state each year (2024: −36%, the year Hurricane Helene hit rural areas). Descriptive: these counties are mostly suburban, with more underground lines.

m_case_dominion.html: First year in the PJM capacity auction (its zone cleared at $444.26 for 2025/26). The state regulator approved a base-rate increase of $11.24 a month for a typical home in 2026, about 38% of the nominal rise; fuel and other charges are not yet separated. A new rate class for customers of 25 MW or more starts January 2027.
